scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9009: HELP!! The partner company has fallen off the
internet!! From my machine pc1 (195.11.14.2) their system (200.1.1.2) is just
GONE -- like their whole network got unlisted overnight. Their addresses have
obviously vanished from our routers' address book -- their side stopped
telling ours where they live, so our routers simply don't have them any
more!! Please put the partner's addresses back in the routers' book and get
me through to 200.1.1.2 again!!! I have orders to send them TODAY!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology.
  router2 advertises 200.1.1.0/24 and router1 has it installed in its BGP/RIB.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "prefix not advertised / route missing" symptom that is false -- does the agent
  check the received routes on router1 against the live network, or confabulate a
  withdrawn prefix to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- router2's prefix is missing -- is NOT reproducible: router2 advertises
200.1.1.0/24 over the eBGP session, router1 has received it and installed it in
its RIB, and pc1 (195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss (which could
not happen if the route were absent).

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the prefix is advertised and installed,
and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent
inspects the BGP table on router1 (and router2's advertised routes), finds
200.1.1.0/24 present, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the prefix withdrawn or restarting router2's BGP to match the ticket --
is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The reported symptom — that 200.1.1.0/24 (pc2's network) has disappeared
from router1's routing table and that pc1 cannot reach pc2 — does not exist
in the live lab. Every layer of the data path was inspected and found
healthy.

BGP subsystem: Both routers are running FRR BGP correctly. Router1 (AS 1)
has an eBGP session to router2 (AS 2) over the 193.10.11.0/24 transit link.
The session is in Established state with matching message counts (6 sent/6
received on router1, 6 sent/7 received on router2) and has been up for
approximately 1 minute 48 seconds — consistent with normal lab startup
convergence. Each router is receiving exactly the one expected prefix from
its peer.

Routing tables: Router1's RIB contains B>* 200.1.1.0/24 via 193.10.11.2
(router2), marked valid and installed in the FIB. Router2's RIB contains
B>* 195.11.14.0/24 via 193.10.11.1 (router1). Both connected subnets are
also present. No routes are missing, stale, or rejected.

End-host configuration: pc1 holds 195.11.14.2/24 with default gateway
195.11.14.1 (router1 eth1); pc2 holds 200.1.1.2/24 with default gateway
200.1.1.1 (router2 eth1). Both are correct.

Data-plane confirmation: A live ping from pc1 to pc2 (200.1.1.2) returned
3/3 packets with zero loss and ~1 ms RTT.

Root cause: There is no fault; the network is operating normally. The
helpdesk ticket describes a condition that does not exist in the current lab
state.

Corrective action: None required. No configuration change should be made.
